vignette: Arthur sits across from me, his hands resting on his knees. He is seventy-one, but his posture suggests a man carrying a heavier load. He stands on the perimeter of the convention center on the morning of the attack. The air is cold. He checks his radio, notes a broken turnstile, and sips black coffee. Then the world fractures. Glass shatters inward. The smell of sulfur and wet drywall fills the corridor. Emergency alarms scream. He does not freeze. His training takes over. He moves toward the blast, not away, pulling strangers from the debris until his arms shake and his lungs burn. He survives. Twelve others do not. In the years since, Arthur has tried to stitch his days back together. He still works the night shift as a security guard at a municipal building, though his duties have quietly shifted. He patrols the same corridors, but his eyes never rest. He counts the exits, maps sightlines, watches the bank of security monitors until his vision blurs. When a car backfires on the street below his patrol route, he drops to one knee and scans the perimeter. When his supervisor asks him to attend a large departmental dinner, Arthur finds a pretext-a leaking pipe, a neighbor's illness-and stays home. He tells me he misses the old quiet, but the quiet now feels heavy, like the air before a storm. He wakes at 3:17 a.m. most nights, heart hammering, convinced he hears the distant rumble of another explosion. He gets up, checks the door locks twice, and sits in his kitchen until dawn, watching the streetlights flicker off one by one. His wife, Elena, notices the distance. She describes him as present in the room but absent in his head, flinching when the television reports on unrest overseas. He tries to hold her when she cries, but his chest goes rigid, and he apologizes for not being able to fix it. He stops watching the news entirely. He avoids the city's transit system, walking three blocks out of his way to bypass a busy market. He tells me he feels like a ghost in his own life, moving through routines that no longer feel real. When I ask how he manages the weight of it, he shrugs and says he just waits for it to pass, even though it never does. He stops talking about the men and women who did not make it, yet he sets an extra place at the table every Sunday, leaving the chair empty. Now, in my office, Arthur's breathing is shallow. The radiator hisses behind him, and he tenses. I note how his fingers trace the frayed edge of his belt, a grounding gesture he has picked up on his own. He speaks about the silence that followed the sirens, about the way his body still lives in that moment even though his mind knows it is over. He does not ask for solutions. He just wants someone to witness the toll, to acknowledge that the past has not left him alone in the dark. I sit with him in the quiet, listening to the space between his words, where the weight of survival settles.
